metric.why: Idle servers burn power, licenses, and depreciation while producing nothing. Fleet utilization is where the money hides in most enterprise estates, and it is the denominator that makes every efficiency metric honest.
metric.definition: The share of provisioned compute doing real work, measured over time rather than at peak.

reading.body:
Server utilization is the share of provisioned compute doing real work, and it is only meaningful when measured over time rather than read at peak.

The definition carries more weight than any single reading of it. A fleet measured at peak looks busy by construction, because peak is the moment demand and provisioned capacity sit closest together. Averaged over time, the same fleet exposes the gap between what was bought and what is used. That gap is not free. Idle servers still draw power, still carry licenses, and still depreciate, so unused capacity is a recurring cost rather than a stored asset.

For AI this is the denominator problem. Any claim about efficiency per unit of compute depends on how much of the provisioned fleet was actually working. Where utilization is low, added capacity is partly a bet on future demand rather than a response to present load, and the power drawn by that idle equipment is being spent ahead of the work it was built for.

What the data does not contain is any value. There is no utilization figure, no fleet size, no time series, and no target. It also does not separate compute doing useful AI work from compute doing any work at all. The metric sits among other capacity questions, stranded power and space per cabinet and floor loading limits, which are physical constraints on the same estate. Utilization says how much of the machine is busy. It does not say whether the building can hold more.
